title: RBAC, Audit Logging, Data Residency & Retention, Secure SDLC, Incident Response, and Compliance Evidence Workflows
author: Aisha Patel
body:
Summary:
This document consolidates Redwood Inference's controls and operational procedures for role-based access control (RBAC) and authentication, audit logging, data residency & retention, secure SDLC practices, incident response (security focused), compliance evidence collection workflows, and risk & exceptions processes. It is intended for engineering, security, product, and compliance stakeholders responsible for design, implementation, and evidence generation for internal and external audits (SOC2, ISO, regulatory assessments).

Scope:
- Applies to all Redwood services (hosted API, Dedicated, Private) and associated control planes, management consoles, internal tooling, and telemetry systems.
- Covers human and machine identities, production and non-production environments, and customer-facing data stores where Redwood has custody.

1) RBAC & Authentication
Overview:
Redwood enforces least-privilege RBAC across all control planes and service interfaces. Access is granted via explicit roles and time-bound policies; privileges for production services are segmented from non-production.

Key concepts and roles:
- Roles: platform-admin, infra-operator, svc-deployer, model-onboarder, security-auditor, support-analyst, billing-reader.
- Role-to-permission mapping: defined in the central IAM catalog (see Appendix A).
- Just-in-time (JIT) elevation: production-sensitive roles require approval via the access request workflow and are granted temporary tokens (max 8 hours).

Authentication and identity providers:
- Primary SSO: Okta (OIDC). All interactive users must authenticate through SSO with MFA (TOTP + hardware key for privileged users).
- Machine identities: short-lived service tokens issued by Vault (mTLS + signed cert rotation).
- Third-party integrations: reviewed and scoped under the integration onboarding checklist (must define least scopes and data flow).

Provisioning and deprovisioning:
- Automated deprovisioning is triggered from HR/SCIM for terminated users; manual checklist for contractors.
- Quarterly access reviews owned by team leads; security-auditor runs automated stale access reports monthly.

2) Audit Logging
Goal:
Provide tamper-evident, queryable audit trails for authentication events, authorization decisions, admin actions, and sensitive data access to support investigations and compliance.

Logging requirements:
- Events captured: auth success/failure, token issuance/rotation, role changes, permission grants/revokes, configuration changes (infra, model pinning, routing policies), data exports, and admin console actions.
- Minimum retention (audit index): 365 days in immutable store; critical security events retained 7 years for enterprise customers on contract.
- Log integrity: logs are forwarded to centralized logging (Kafka -> ELK/Datadog/Long-term S3 archive) with signed checksums and periodic immutability snapshots.

Access to logs:
- Only security-auditor, infra-operator (read-only), and compliance roles may query raw audit data; queries are themselves logged.

Alerting and monitoring:
- Real-time alerts on anomalous auth patterns (geo anomalies, impossible travel), privilege escalations, and suspicious data export attempts. SLO for alerting pipeline: 99% of high-severity alerts delivered within 60 seconds.

3) Data Residency & Retention
Residency controls:
- Customer regions: data stores are region-tagged; customer resources are provisioned in requested regions where supported.
- Cross-region replication: default disabled for customer data unless explicitly permitted in contract; all cross-region transfers documented and logged.

Retention policy:
- Configuration and metadata: retained for 7 years for recovery and auditability.
- Customer content (input prompts, generated outputs): default retention 30 days for hosted API; customers can opt into longer retention or zero-retention options.
- Embeddings and vector indexes: retention configurable per-customer, default 90 days unless contractually extended.

Data deletion requests:
- Deletion workflow: request received -> validation -> scheduled deletion -> deletion confirmation logged. SLA: complete deletions within 30 days for most requests; expedited deletions (7 days) available for compliance needs.

4) Secure SDLC
Principles:
- Security gates integrated into CI/CD with automated static analysis, dependency scanning, secret scanning, container image scanning, and runtime fuzzing for critical services.
- Shift-left testing: threat modeling and security requirements at PR stage for all changes touching model serving, control plane, authentication, or data handling.

Gates and tooling:
- Required checks: unit tests, integration tests, SAST, SCA, license checks, infra-plan linter, and terraform policy checks (OPA/Gatekeeper).
- Pull request policy: all PRs require at least one security review for changes to sensitive components; changes to RBAC, audit or retention policies require sign-off from the security owner.
- Release process: canary rollout with automated canary analysis against production metrics and observability runbooks before full rollout.

Third-party code and models:
- Vendor risk assessment required for third-party models or SDKs that are deployed in production. Signed SBOMs maintained for all service images.

5) Incident Response — Security Procedures
Objectives:
- Contain, eradicate, and recover from security incidents while preserving evidence for forensic review and compliance reporting.

Detection and triage:
- Incident detection sources: IDS/IPS, EDR alerts, anomaly detection in request patterns, audit log monitoring, customer reports.
- Triage timeline: acknowledge within 15 minutes, initial classification (severity 1-4) within 60 minutes.

Response playbook highlights:
1. Initial containment: revoke compromised service tokens, isolate affected nodes (network ACLs), and apply emergency ACLs to control-plane.
2. Evidence preservation: snapshot affected VMs/containers, collect relevant logs (from immutable archive), export signed checksums to forensic bucket (WORM).
3. Root cause analysis: dedicated incident commander assigns scope and owners; security and infra teams execute RCA and document timelines.
4. Customer communication: pre-approved notification templates; legal and privacy consult for regulated data exposures.
5. Remediation & follow-up: action items tracked in post-incident plan; update runbooks and security controls.

Post-incident reporting:
- Postmortem published within 10 business days for Sev1/Sev2 with redacted timelines for public disclosure; internal RCA artifacts retained per evidence retention policy.

6) Compliance Evidence Workflows
Evidence catalog:
- Standard artifacts: access review reports, audit logs, change control records, SAST/SCA scan outputs, architecture diagrams, threat models, SOC2 evidence bundles.
- Evidence owner: each control mapped to an evidence owner (security, infra, platform, or product). The controlbook maps owners and artifact locations.

Evidence collection process:
1. Request & intake: compliance team opens evidence request ticket with required artifacts and timeframe.
2. Owner assembly: evidence owner compiles artifacts, provides context, and certifies accuracy.
3. Validation: security reviews artifacts for completeness; if gaps found, remediation tasks created with target dates.
4. Delivery: artifacts uploaded to secure evidence repository with access logs and versioning.

Automation and tooling:
- Automated evidence pulls: access reviews, audit log extracts, and CI/CD gate artifacts are exported on schedule to the evidence repo.
- Evidence retention: aligned with audit logging retention and contractual requirements.

7) Risk & Exceptions Process
Risk classification:
- Low/Medium/High risk buckets with documented acceptance criteria and compensating controls.

Exception workflow:
1. Submit exception request: owner documents scope, rationale, compensating controls, and proposed expiration.
2. Security review board: evaluates technical risk and business justification; may require mitigation plan and monitoring.
3. Approval: approved exceptions issued with time-bound TTL (max 90 days for High risk; extension requires re-approval).
4. Tracking: all exceptions logged in centralized risk register and reviewed in quarterly risk reviews.

Mandatory compensating controls for high-risk exceptions:
- Extra audit logging, continuous monitoring with elevated alerting thresholds, and mandatory quarterly attestation by the owning team.

8) Ownership & Cadence
- Security (owner): maintain this document, run quarterly reviews, and own security-audit evidence readiness.
- Team leads: quarterly access reviews, monthly compliance checklist confirmations.
- Compliance: coordinates evidence requests, audit timelines, and external assessments.

Appendices
A. Example RBAC mapping (abbreviated):
- platform-admin: manage infra, view billing, override quotas.
- infra-operator: manage cluster, deploy infra changes, read logs.
- svc-deployer: deploy service artifacts to staging; prod deploy requires JIT.

B. Audit event JSON example (abbreviated):
{
  "ts": "2027-08-01T12:34:56Z",
  "event": "role_grant",
  "actor": "alice@redwood.com",
  "target": "svc-deployer",
  "details": "granted by approval #1234"
}

C. Retention summary table (plain text):
- Audit logs (security index): 365 days; critical events: 7 years
- Config/metadata: 7 years
- Customer content (default): 30 days (opt-in longer)
- Embeddings: 90 days default (configurable)
